paper.title: Sharp Dichotomies for Regret Minimization in Metric Spaces

settings.definition_quote: we define the double feedback, where in each round the algorithm selects two strategies: the ``bet" for which it receives the payoff, and the ``free peek". After the round, the payoffs are revealed for both strategies.

unmapped: payoff functions are i.i.d. random functions in [0,1]^X with Lipschitz mean

In each round an algorithm is presented with an i.i.d. sample from $\prob$.

symbols.f_T: any function in omega(log T); constant depends on the instance

conditions: completion of X is compact and countable

source.label: thm:main-MAB
source.quote: Consider the Lipschitz MAB problem on a fixed metric space $(X,d)$. Then the following dichotomy holds: either the problem is $f(t)$-tractable for every $f\in \omega(\log t)$, or it is not $g(t)$-tractable for any $g\in o(\sqrt{t})$.  In fact, the former occurs if and only if the completion of $X$ is a compact metric space with countably many points.

results.notes: Tractability statement: for each f in omega(log t) an algorithm with instance-dependent O(f) regret exists. Proved via Theorem 4.1(a) (compact well-orderable spaces) plus reduction to completion.

conditions: completion of X is not both compact and countable

source.label: thm:main-MAB
source.quote: either the problem is $f(t)$-tractable for every $f\in \omega(\log t)$, or it is not $g(t)$-tractable for any $g\in o(\sqrt{t})$.

results.notes: Precisely: for every algorithm and every g=o(sqrt t), some instance has regret not O_I(g(t)) (holds infinitely often, not for all t). Recorded as Omega(sqrt T).

source.label: thm:logT
source.quote: For every infinite metric space $(X,d)$, the Lipschitz MAB problem on $(X,d)$ is not $(\log t)$-tractable.

results.notes: Actual statement is stronger than Omega(log T): no algorithm has O_I(log t) regret on all instances, i.e. regret is omega(log t) on some instance.

conditions: completion of X is compact and countable

source.label: thm:main-experts
source.quote: The Lipschitz experts problem on a fixed metric space $(X,d)$ is either $1$-tractable, even with double feedback, or it is not $g(t)$-tractable for any $g\in o(\sqrt{t})$, even with full feedback. The former occurs if and only if the completion of $X$ is a compact metric space with countably many points.

conditions: completion of X is not both compact and countable

source.label: thm:main-experts
source.quote: or it is not $g(t)$-tractable for any $g\in o(\sqrt{t})$, even with full feedback.

results.notes: Holds even with full feedback (hence also bandit). Instance-specific, infinitely-often sense.

source.label: thm:lower-bound
source.quote: Consider the Lipschitz experts problem on a metric space $(X,d)$ which has a perfect subspace. Then the problem is not $g$-tractable for any $g\in o(\sqrt{t})$. In fact, a much stronger result holds: there exist a distribution $\mathcal{P}$ over problem instances $\mu$ such that for any experts algorithm \A\ we have ... $\Pr_{\mu\in\mathcal{P}} [ R_{(\A,\,\mu)}(t) = O_{\mu}(g(t)) ] = 0$.

results.notes: Stronger form: almost every instance from a distribution over instances fails o(sqrt t) regret. Applies to experts algorithms, hence also bandit algorithms.

symbols.f_T: some function in o(T) depending on the metric space

source.label: thm:boundary-of-tractability
source.quote: The Lipschitz experts problem on a fixed metric space $(X,d)$ is either $f(t)$-tractable for some $f\in o(t)$, even in the bandit setting, or it is not $g(t)$-tractable for any $g\in o(t)$, even with full feedback. The former occurs if and only if the completion of $X$ is a compact metric space.

results.notes: Upper bound holds in the bandit setting.

conditions: completion of X is not compact

source.label: thm:boundary-of-tractability
source.quote: or it is not $g(t)$-tractable for any $g\in o(t)$, even with full feedback. The former occurs if and only if the completion of $X$ is a compact metric space.

results.notes: Linear regret (infinitely often, instance-specific) even with full feedback; Lemma 7.2 gives the a.s. version over a random instance distribution.

symbols.eps_T: min{2^{-k}: T <= s_k}, s_k the cumulative phase lengths tuned to covering numbers; eps_T -> 0

tuning: phase lengths t_i = min(t*_i, t*_{i+1}, 2 sum_{j<i} t_j)

source.quote: Consider the Lipschitz MAB problem on a compact and complete metric space $(X,d)$. Then $R_\A(t) \leq 5\, \eps(t)\, t$, where $\eps(t) = \min\{ 2^{-k}:\, t\leq s_k\}$ and $s_k = \sum_{i=1}^k\, t_i$. In particular, $R_\A(t) = o(t)$.

results.notes: Bound is worst-case over Lipschitz instances given the metric space; dependence labelled instance-dependent loosely since eps(t) depends on metric covering numbers (not instance). Proof hides O() constants from UCB1.

tuning: k_t = floor(sqrt(f(t)/log t)), n_t = floor(k_t log t), phases of length 2^(2^i)

source.label: thm:main-alg
source.quote: Consider a compact well-orderable metric space $(X,d)$. Then: (a) the Lipschitz MAB problem on $(X,d)$ is $f$-tractable for every $f\in\omega(\log t)$; (b) the Lipschitz experts problem on $(X,d)$ is 1-tractable, even with a double feedback.

results.notes: Part (a). Requires covering oracle and ordering oracle. Theorem 6.3(a) gives the same guarantee for compact spaces of finite Cantor-Bendixson rank using only per-rank covering oracles (algorithm a3).

tuning: k_t = n_t = floor(sqrt t), phases of length 2^i

source.label: thm:main-alg
source.quote: (b) the Lipschitz experts problem on $(X,d)$ is 1-tractable, even with a double feedback.

results.notes: Part (b). Theorem 6.3(b) gives same for finite Cantor-Bendixson rank with covering oracles only.

conditions: (X,d) compact with LIM(X,N) empty for some finite N (finite Cantor-Bendixson rank)

source.label: thm:lim-decomposable
source.quote: Consider the Lipschitz MAB/experts problem on a compact metric space $(X,d)$ such that $\LimSet_N(X)=\emptyset$ for some $N$. ... Then: (a) the Lipschitz MAB problem on $(X,d)$ is $f$-tractable for every $f\in\omega(\log t)$; (b) the Lipschitz experts problem on $(X,d)$ is 1-tractable, even with a double feedback.

results.notes: Part (a); access only via covering oracles for each X_i. Part (b) gives O(1) with double feedback (same as r11 under these conditions).

symbols.b_par: algorithm parameter b > LCD(X), the log-covering dimension of X

tuning: delta = T^{-1/(b+2)} per phase of length T=2^i

source.label: thm:ffproblem-naive
source.quote: Consider the \FFproblem\ on a metric space $(X,d)$. For each $b>\LCD(X)$, algorithm $\NaiveExp(b)$ achieves regret $R(t) = O(t^{1-1/(b+2)})$.

results.notes: Constant may depend on metric space (sufficiently large T). Dependence labelled worst_case over instances of the fixed metric space.

source.label: thm:ulproblem-naive
source.quote: Consider the \ULproblem\ with full feedback. Fix a metric space $(X,d)$. For each $b>\LCD(X)$ such that $b\geq 2$, $\NaiveExp(b-2)$ achieves regret $R(t) = O(t^{1-1/b})$.

source.label: thm:experts-MaxMinLCD-body
source.quote: Fix a metric space $(X,d)$ and let $b=\MaxMinLCD(X)$. The \FFproblem\ on $(X,d)$ is $(t^\gamma)$-tractable for any $\gamma> \tfrac{b+1}{b+2}$, and not $(t^\gamma)$-tractable for any $\gamma < \tfrac{b-1}{b}$.

results.notes: Same as Theorem 1.6. Upper bound proof only sketched; algorithm requires depth and covering oracles for a transfinite LCD decomposition.
Lower bound of Theorem 9.1/1.6, stated to hold even for the uniformly Lipschitz experts problem (hence also full-feedback Lipschitz experts). Means regret not O_I(t^gamma) for some instance.

source.label: thm:experts-MaxMinLCD-unif-body
source.quote: Consider the \ULproblem\ with full feedback. Fix a metric space $(X,d)$ with uncountably many points, and let $b=\MaxMinLCD(X)$. The problem on $(X,d)$ is $(t^\gamma)$-tractable for any $\gamma> \max(\tfrac{b-1}{b},\, \tfrac12)$, and not $(t^\gamma)$-tractable for any $\gamma < \max(\tfrac{b-1}{b},\, \tfrac12)$.

results.notes: Same as Theorem 1.7. Upper bound proof sketched.
Combines the MaxMinLCD lower bound with the sqrt(t) lower bound for uncountable spaces (which contain a perfect subspace after completion).
